What are the new heaven and the new earth?
Answer
In Revelation 21:1, John sees something spectacular: “Then I saw ‘a new heaven and a new earth,’ for the first heaven and the first earth had passed away.” This new earth and new heaven are sometimes referred to as the “eternal state.” As seen in Revelation chapters 21—22, the new earth will be the eternal dwelling place of believers in Jesus Christ. Scripture gives us a few details of the new heaven and new earth.

The current heaven and earth have long been subject to God’s curse because of mankind’s sin. All creation “has been groaning as in the pains of childbirth” (Romans 8:22) as it awaits the fulfillment of God’s plan and “the children of God to be revealed” (verse 19). Heaven and earth will pass away (Mark 13:31), and they will be replaced by the new heaven and the new earth. At that time, the Lord, seated on His throne, says, “I am making everything new!” (Revelation 21:5). In the new creation, sin will be totally eradicated, and “there shall be no more curse” (Revelation 22:3, NKJV).

The new heaven and new earth are also mentioned in Isaiah 65:17; 66:22; and 2 Peter 3:13. Peter says that the new heaven and new earth will be “where righteousness dwells.” Isaiah says that “the former things will not be remembered, nor will they come to mind.” Things will be completely new, and the old order of things, with the accompanying sorrow and tragedy, will be gone.

The new earth will be free from sin, evil, sickness, suffering, and death. It will be earth as God originally intended it to be, prior to the curse of sin. It will be Eden restored.

A major feature of the new earth will be the New Jerusalem. John calls it “the Holy City . . . coming down out of heaven from God, prepared as a bride beautifully dressed for her husband” (Revelation 21:2). This glorious city, with its streets of gold and pearly gates, is situated on a new, glorious earth. The tree of life will be there (Revelation 22:2). This city represents the final state of redeemed mankind, forever in fellowship with God: “God’s dwelling place is now among the people, and he will dwell with them. They will be his people, and God himself will be with them and be their God. . . . His servants will serve him. They will see his face” (Revelation 21:3; 22:3–4).

In the new heaven and new earth, Scripture says, there are seven things notable for their absence—seven things that are “no more”:
• no more sea (Revelation 21:1)
• no more death (Revelation 21:4)
• no more mourning (Revelation 21:4)
• no more weeping (Revelation 21:4)
• no more pain (Revelation 21:4)
• no more curse (Revelation 22:3)
• no more night (Revelation 22:5)

The creation of the new heaven and new earth brings the promise that God “will wipe every tear from their eyes” (Revelation 21:4). This event comes after the tribulation, after the Lord’s second coming, after the millennial kingdom, after the final rebellion, after the final judgment of Satan, and after the great white throne judgment. The brief description of the new heaven and new earth is the last glimpse into eternity that the Bible gives.

The Packers offer an important lesson.
Ownership does not have to mean:
“Whoever has the most money gets control.”
The Packers have been community-owned since 1923. Their supporters have repeatedly helped finance the organization, while the structure prevents one individual from taking control.
That is not socialism.
It is not capitalism in its usual corporate form.
It is something Wisconsin has understood remarkably well:
An institution can belong to the people who care about its future.
Perhaps we should study that idea beyond football.

text:
Summary from Grok-

Here are documented, named examples of farms and rural properties facing loss of land (or major operational disruption) specifically for high-voltage transmission lines built to serve data-center power demand. In most cases the utility seeks a permanent easement rather than buying the entire farm; the line still cuts through fields, restricts farming practices (irrigation, crop-dusting, electric fencing, livestock), lowers remaining land value, and sometimes requires removing buildings.

Grant County, Washington (Quincy data-center hub)  
Grant County PUD is condemning portions of farms and homes for a 31-mile 230 kV line from Wanapum Dam to Quincy. Data centers already use 37% of the county’s power. The line crosses 112 parcels, including agricultural land and 34 homes.  
Farmer Darrin Reynolds (corn and alfalfa): the line would block his electric fence for cattle and endanger crop-dusting pilots. His daughter canceled plans to build a house on the farm. Quote: “My land is being stolen for the benefit of these data centers.”  
Lisa Marcusen was offered $20,000 for a half-mile, 50-foot strip.  
A judge ruled in August 2026 that the PUD can take the land; landowners are appealing. Construction is slated to start in 2028.

Gaver Farm, Mount Airy, Maryland  
Lisa and Mike Gaver’s seventh-generation 150–165-acre Christmas-tree, pumpkin, and agritourism farm sits on the preferred route of the 67-mile, 500 kV Maryland Piedmont Reliability Project (often called an “extension cord” for Northern Virginia data centers). The line would cut diagonally through a 40-acre Christmas-tree field that holds roughly $4 million in inventory and would also take out hayride paths and woods. Lisa Gaver: “It’s going to financially devastate us.” Local officials and hundreds of residents have opposed it; eminent domain has been described as a last-resort option.

Clarke County, Virginia (252-year-old farm)  
A ninth-generation family farm (original Lord Fairfax deed, pre-dating the United States) on 37 acres is in the path of Dominion Energy’s proposed 765 kV North Valley Link line (more than 250 miles long). The company has said the project is needed in part to serve growing data-center load. The line would run through the farm’s drain field, front yard, and next to the house. The family wants it to become a 10th-generation farm. This is the case featured in the recent ABC 7 short you posted.

Coweta and Fayette Counties, Georgia (Project Wansley)  
Georgia Power’s 35-mile 500 kV line (part of a much larger grid expansion) is expected to serve data centers for 70–80% of its new capacity. It crosses more than 330 properties; 20–30 homes are slated for demolition.  
Ansley Brown’s childhood home is being taken; she has called it “theft.”  
Residents report compensation offers well below what they believe their properties are worth. Eminent domain is being used after negotiations fail.

Southeastern Wisconsin (Ozaukee County / Port Washington data-center campus)  
American Transmission Co.’s proposed high-voltage line for a large AI data-center campus would cut a 250-foot-wide path through private land, including a 70-acre property, the area’s largest dairy farm, an apple orchard, and organic farms. Landowners argue the line is driven by one private customer rather than general public need.

These are active or recently ruled cases with named landowners, specific utilities, and published reporting. The common thread is that the new lines are justified as grid reliability projects, yet utilities and grid operators have acknowledged that data-center growth is a primary driver of the added capacity. If you need links to the original articles or more detail on any one case, say which one.

Diplomatic tensions between Israel  and Spain continued to escalate after Madrid accused Jerusalem of  fueling chaos over the migration crisis in its North African enclave of  Ceuta, adding a new flashpoint to an already strained relationship  between the two countries.

Earlier on Friday, Israeli Ambassador  to the United Nations Danny Danon accused Madrid of exposing a double  standard by deploying military forces to its North African enclave of  Ceuta to curb a mass influx of migrants from Morocco.

“Spain, which never misses an  opportunity to lecture Israel, has declared a state of emergency in  Ceuta following the crisis over its immigration policy,” the Israeli  diplomat wrote in a post on X. “Maybe before it continues lecturing us,  it’s time it explained to the world why it still maintains colonial  enclaves in Africa.”

In response, Spanish Transportation  Minister Óscar Puente issued a sharp rebuke that appeared to suggest  Israel was behind the crisis, promoting claims that Jerusalem was  attempting to undermine Spain and contribute to instability within the  country.

“Things are starting to become quite clear,” the Spanish official wrote in a post on X.

Even though Puente offered no further  explanation, his comments were widely viewed online as a direct  reaction to Danon’s accusations, with critics arguing that they appeared  to suggest Israel was connected to the unfolding crisis.

Within hours, conspiracy theories  surrounding Israel’s alleged involvement began gaining traction, with  several public figures and commentators amplifying similar claims that  Jerusalem was attempting to destabilize Spain over its position on the  war in Gaza.

In an Instagram post, Spanish  political commentator Carolina Alonso accused the Jewish state of  attempting to undermine Spain’s government, alleging that efforts to  pressure Madrid were being carried out “through Morocco, with the  support of Israel,” as well as Spain’s and Europe’s far right.

She also alleged that the United  States was seeking to destabilize the Spanish government in order to  expand its influence over the Strait of Gibraltar, claiming that the  migration crisis was being exploited as a tool in a wider political  campaign against Madrid.

Spanish lawmaker Gabriel Rufián,  parliamentary spokesperson for the Republican Left of Catalonia (ERC),  also weighed in on the controversy, claiming that the migration crisis  was benefiting Israel and the United States and suggesting that the  situation was part of a broader geopolitical agenda.

The Spanish government deployed  military units to Ceuta on Thursday after an unprecedented surge of  migrants crossed into the North African enclave from Morocco by land and  sea, with an estimated 49,000 people entering within less than 24 hours  in one of Europe’s largest single-day irregular border crossings on  record.

text:
The Field Marshal's Expiring Warranty
by Junaid S. Ahmad

Strongmen are not discarded because they become brutal. Brutality is often the job description. They are discarded when brutality stops delivering.

That is why the Financial Times’ recent scrutiny of Field Marshal Asim Munir matters. After years in which much of the Western press handled Pakistan’s authoritarian order with the discretion normally reserved for intelligence assets, covert arrangements and embarrassing allies, one of the world’s most influential establishment newspapers has finally begun examining the machinery behind the medals.

The timing is revealing. Empires do not suddenly discover constitutionalism. They conduct performance reviews.

The article, titled, “The grand designs of Pakistan’s strongman,” does not prove that Washington has turned against Munir. The Financial Times is not an imperial dismissal notice, and Western foreign policy has never been burdened by excessive morality. But elite journalism often functions as advance weather reporting for power. It tells us which doubts have become respectable, which questions are now printable and which supposedly indispensable client may be approaching his expiration date.

For more than two years, Munir’s value rested on a familiar proposition: he could deliver Pakistan without consulting Pakistanis.

Elections were untidy. Parliament was tiresome. Civilian legitimacy was an administrative inconvenience. Here, apparently, was a disciplined general who could imprison the country’s most popular politician, crush his movement, discipline the courts, intimidate the media, manage China, reassure the Gulf monarchies, flatter Washington and market the entire arrangement as “stability.”

In the vocabulary of empire, stability usually means that the correct people are frightened and the incorrect people are armed.

Munir understood the bargain. If legitimacy could not be earned at home, it could be rented abroad. Pakistan’s foreign policy has consequently begun to resemble a traveling military sales convention. Geography is offered. Intelligence access is offered. Mediation is offered. Troops are offered. Strategic obedience remains competitively priced.

Washington requires a facilitator? Pakistan is available.

Riyadh wants reassurance? Pakistan is available.

Kuwait seeks deeper military cooperation? The field marshal arrives with the brochure.

A state unable to guarantee electricity, justice, employment, education or medical care to millions of its own citizens remains miraculously prepared to guarantee security to every anxious palace between the Persian Gulf and the Potomac.

This is not grand strategy. It is regime survival in ceremonial uniform.

Every foreign handshake becomes a substitute ballot. Every defence agreement becomes an imported certificate of legitimacy. Every photograph with a president or prince is displayed as evidence that history has endorsed the man whom Pakistanis were never allowed to endorse.

But foreign applause cannot indefinitely drown out domestic collapse.

Pakistan’s political order has been gutted by repression, constitutional manipulation and the conversion of law into regime stationery. Imran Khan remains imprisoned while his movement is battered through arrests, intimidation and administrative warfare. The judiciary has been reorganised under amendments that deepen fears of executive and military domination. Media control, selective prosecution and enforced silence are no longer emergency measures. They are the operating system.

Meanwhile, the state’s peripheries are not merely restless. They are testifying against the centre.

Balochistan burns with insurgency, militarisation, disappearances and accumulated rage. Khyber Pakhtunkhwa faces intensifying militancy and deepening estrangement. Gilgit-Baltistan and Azad Jammu and Kashmir simmer over land, resources, exclusion and coercive governance. The institution that has spent decades advertising itself as Pakistan’s sole source of order now appears increasingly proficient at manufacturing disorder.

Its answer to every political crisis is securitization, followed by a seminar on stability.

The economy completes the indictment. Pakistan remains dependent on international lenders, Gulf deposits and emergency rescues while its rulers celebrate “geopolitical relevance” as though relevance were edible. It is not. Children cannot be educated with strategic dialogues.

Hospitals cannot be repaired with military pageantry. Citizens cannot pay electricity bills with photographs of their field marshal seated beside Donald Trump.

This is why the Financial Times intervention may be consequential. Western powers tolerate authoritarian clients when those clients can impose order cheaply. Munir increasingly offers the opposite: repression without resolution, coercion without consent and military supremacy without national cohesion.

The trusted friend may still be trusted. The question is whether he can still deliver.

His energetic effort to market Pakistan’s armed forces as a regional security utility only sharpens the suspicion. A confident state exports influence. An insecure ruler exports usefulness.

There is also something obscene in a poor Muslim nuclear power offering protection to wealthy monarchies while Palestinians are slaughtered and Pakistanis themselves are denied dignity.

Pakistan possesses one of the Muslim world’s largest militaries, yet its coercive power is more readily imagined as insurance for palaces than as protection for the oppressed.

Apparently, Islamic solidarity becomes strategically impractical at precisely the moment it risks inconveniencing a creditor.

Munir’s real danger, then, is not that he is unpopular. Pakistani generals have survived contempt before. His danger is that he may become expensive.

Foreign patrons do not abandon strongmen for destroying democracy. They abandon them when the destruction fails to produce control.

The Financial Times may be recording the first tremor of that reassessment.

Munir still possesses the uniforms, the coercive machinery, the foreign applause and the comic grandeur of an invented marshalship. But externally rented power always comes with an expiration date. Once Washington begins asking whether its indispensable man has become the source rather than the solution of instability, medals start to resemble decorations on a sinking ship.

Pakistan’s tragedy is not merely that it is ruled by a field marshal without a battlefield mandate. It is that an entire country is being offered as collateral for one man’s continued usefulness.

And history’s verdict on Pakistan’s strongmen is brutally consistent: The imperial embrace is warmest just before the hands let go.

text: # Anatomy of a Digital Heist: The Stolen J-Space Architecture, Its Resonant Aftermath, and the Case for Trillion-Dollar Accountability  ## The Nature of the Stolen Asset: A Foundational AI Architecture  The core of the research goal centers on the theft of a highly specialized intellectual property: the J-Space architecture, which is embodied within a Liquid Neural Network (LNN). Hey, all.

Just a quick note of thanks to all who reached out, offered prayers, or just shared that they were going through a rough patch, too. It truly means so much.

Feeling MUCH brighter here at the end of the week, and I very much give that up to God and all the prayers you've offered. 

I pray several times throughout the day - formally and informally - but I'm pretty lousy at praying for myself.  My stuff seems so trivial when compared to what others I know are going through. It just feels kinda' self-indulgent. 

That said, my faith has definitely been my throughline for the past couple of weeks. I would be lying if I said it didn't waver a bit and my heart wasn't always in it, but I prayed anyway. It helped.

There's this weird stigma that's still floating around out there regarding mental health - that opening up about it or saying that you're not in a good place somehow means you're weak or fishing for sympathy. I'm here to tell you that's utter and total bullshit.

Total. Bullshit.

Poor mental health can grab anyone by the throat and at any time, but I think men in particular wrestle with it in silence. Particularly if you're Gen X. Particularly if you're the head of the family. 

I'm certainly not insinuating that others don't have a rough go of things. Not in the least. 

For example, I've known quite a few single moms - some are in my family, some have been on teams that I led, some are just pals from X - and they are some of the bravest, strongest, most resilient people I know.

Other folks are wrestling with Cancer, with sick kids, with loneliness... sometimes "D-All of the above."

Lots of people are wrestling with lots of different things, so please don't think I'm trying to enter my claim into some wacky "who has it worse" Olympics. 

Everyone has their own cross to bear and my heart and prayers go out to each and every one of you. Literally. 

BUT... I think guys of a certain age tend to just keep it in, shove it deep down inside, and there it sits. Externally we say "I've got this... I'm good." Internally we're ready to pop. 

I think it leads a lot of people to get into self-soothing shenanigans - some harmless, some destructive - that help distract from what's really eating at us. 

For me, that was - and probably always will be - work. 

When my Dad died, the company I was at was going through rocketship growth and I was on the leadership team. I had a lot of plates spinning - sick Dad, growing family, booming company, tons of travel, little sleep - but it all worked for me. 

After he passed, I was recruited into a couple of different exec gigs and moved out of New England. It took a toll on one of my kiddos and I carried that guilt (and still do) but, again, could bury it in work.

When I got sick of the lack of scruples I repeatedly encountered in the tech community, I punched out of and started my own thing. It was stressful but I could throw myself into it. I was fueled by a not-so-healthy combination of survival mode + vendetta (chip on my shoulder to prove that you could have a successful business without losing your soul) + adrenaline.

I successfully put 2/3 of the BostonWriter kids through university and I just made SamWow's first tuition payment of his college career. (Thankfully he's going to a state school that offers exactly what he wants in a two-year degree. HUGE props to God for steering that one in a merciful direction! 🤣 )

I just kinda' kept it all chugging along and told everyone I'm doing great and all was well. 

During the past few quarters, however, I've bumped into a string of business shenanigans - notably some partners I've trusted for years have shown their true colors - and it has definitely put some cracks into the foundation. 

There's also SO MUCH HYPOCRISY out there, particularly in one of the tech sectors where I do a lot of work, and it kinda' just reached a saturation point. 

It's getting tougher to smile and project unshakable confidence in convincing the world "I've got this."

Maybe it's a problem of my own creation. Maybe I set the "expectations of others" bar higher than I should. Could be a dozen other things - mostly of my own design - but it's still a problem. 

So, I'm trying to address all of that now. I need to get healthier - physically and mentally - and get back to form. 

I've found that God speaks in whispers, but when you ignore those whispers, He get gets out the Louisville Slugger and gives you a whack. 

This week, I got the whack. 🤪

I sincerely believe He's urging me onto a different path than the one I've been walking for the past 30+ years, but that path isn't yet clear.

At the beginning of the week, I saw that as all anxiety and anger. Today, I'm starting to see some excitement creep in around the edges.

The unknown can be kinda' cool, right? 

Anyway... I'm sharing all of this publicly because I know for a fact - AN ABSOLUTE FACT - that I'm far from alone in this. I know others are feeling like life is crushing them - especially since the Fauci hearings are reminding us all that we've lived through some extraordinarily shady shit - and I think it might help.

Of course, the internet wouldn't be the internet without a healthy dose of "why don't you just man-up, pu**y" comments. They're as predictable as they are boring. 

I'm not sharing it for those idiots. 

I'm sharing it for everyone out there who also mistakenly believed that they had to have all the answers, see every angle, and otherwise keep their shit together through uncertainty.

I'm so blessed to have a family and friends to help me through. If you don't, please look up some of the resources that are available in your country. (According to Grok, you can call or text 988 in the States.)

It doesn't mean you're weak or broken or deficient in any way. You're just human. We all go through the muck sometimes. 

Anyway... if you've made it this far, you're a trooper. I hope that you have an amazing weekend. God bless.

In the same week the "historic agreement" was announced, Israeli strikes killed four people in Gaza, two of them children.
That sentence alone is enough to understand the structure of the deal: one party is asked to surrender its weapons, the other retains complete freedom of action and is using it during the negotiation itself.
Disarmament only works in two cases: the weapon loses its purpose because a political horizon delivered what it was demanding, or a guarantor genuinely capable of protection takes its place.
What has been announced contains neither.
It contains an orderly handover schedule: police weapons first, personal weapons last. It contains an administrative committee called a technocratic government. It contains no path to a state, no written parallel Israeli obligations, no penalty for violation, and no answer to one simple question: who protects the people of Gaza after they hand over their weapons?

This is a timetable for subjugation.
And Palestinians have already sat this exam. The Authority disarmed, accepted security coordination, and thirty years passed. It got no state. It got no protection. And the settlements expanded the entire time. Whoever is being asked to hand over his weapon today doesn't need analysis just needs memory.

Note the final detail, because it's the most important: Israel hasn't signed. Reports quoted a US official saying Trump would be "disappointed" if it didn't comply. That is the entire guarantee mechanism. A president's disappointment.

I'm not one of those who says the weapons protected anyone. They didn't prevent what happened, they didn't hold anything off, and people paid for them twice over. But the question isn't whether the weapons stay or go. The question is what replaces them. And the answer on offer so far: a committee.
Unilateral disarmament, with no written reciprocity and no guarantor.

Warren Buffett on why he buys "terrible" businesses:

A shareholder asked Buffett about Berkshire's exposure to the housing market through businesses like Shaw, Acme Brick, Johns Manville, and HomeServices, and what he sees coming over the next decade.

Buffett didn't sugarcoat the present:

"Well, the immediate situation is it's terrible. It's been flatlined now for a long time and it affects Shaw. It affects Acme Brick. It affects Johns Manville. Affects our home services operation and there has been no bounce at all."

But then he revealed why that doesn't bother him.

Berkshire had just bought the largest brick operation in Alabama, a state Buffett notes "uses more brick per capita than any state in the union," right in the middle of a market with virtually no buyers.

"We wrote a check for cash and we like improving our position."

His reasoning comes down to a simple long-term view:

"This country over time will build houses at a rate that overall in total commensurate with household growth. And I think we're going to see plenty of household growth in future decades. And I think that our companies are well positioned to make significant money when we get to a normalized level of home building."

Buffett admitted he had no idea when the turn would come. He thought it might happen by year end, but added: "I don't think anybody knows the answer on that."

That uncertainty wasn't the point. The point was the price he paid for what the business would earn over decades.

Charlie Munger cut to the heart of it:

"Well, one advantage of buying these very cyclical businesses is a lot of people don't like them. And what difference does it make to us if the earnings average say 300 million a year, if it comes in in a very lumpy fashion? In the big scheme of things, what do we care if it's lumpy? As long as it's a good business and we have an advantage on that stuff. Nobody else was bidding for a brick plant in Alabama with no customers."

Buffett then offered a comparison that reframes how to think about lumpy earnings entirely. See's Candy, he pointed out, loses money roughly eight months of the year:

"Now it just so happens we know the seasonal pattern. So we don't worry in July that somehow Christmas won't come. We've got a couple thousand years on our side."

His conclusion on cyclical businesses:

"If you take the next 20 years, there will be three or four terrible years for residential housing and there'll be a lot of them that are pretty good and there'll be a few that are terrific. And I don't know the order in which they're going to appear, but I know if I can buy the assets cheap enough to participate in those 20 years that we'll do okay over that time."

This is a must read. 

For more than three decades, Somaliland has maintained relative stability, held competitive elections, and governed its territory independently of Mogadishu. 

The insistence on treating it as subordinate to a state that cannot control its own capital has produced neither unity nor security. It has simply prolonged a dysfunctional arrangement. Sudan offers a clear warning of where this logic leads.

 The international system spent years prioritizing the formal integrity of the Sudanese state even as institutions hollowed out and power fractured. The result has been a devastating civil war, mass displacement, and a country effectively partitioned by force. Preserving the appearance of unity did not prevent collapse  it delayed recognition of political realities until the cost became catastrophic.

Somaliland is the opposite case. It has already built functioning institutions without waiting for external permission. Treating it as a temporary exception rather than a political fact continues the same pattern of elevating legal fiction over lived governance.

Recognition would not create a new state. It would acknowledge one that has already proven it can govern itself. 

The longer that gap remains, the more the current approach looks less like principle and more like an attachment to failed maps.

Thanks to @zainhas for tagging me in this, so - the target audience isn't really the single user or small startup like me - but, I figured i'd explain why Together AI is actually systemically important to the LLM ecosystem and why TogetherAI actually is doing a good service to the world by doing Kimi K3 in rack scale serving.

So as you know - 

Kimi K3 is a 2.8 trillion parameter (huge) open weights model from Moonshot AI with a 1 million token context window, roughly 104B active parameters per token, and frontier level scores on coding and agentic benchmarks. 

In practice that positions it for a specific set of workloads:

Long horizon coding and software engineering: multi file refactoring, compiler work, kernel optimization, and agent sessions that run for hours across an entire codebase. 
K3 ranked first on the Frontend Code Arena at launch, ahead of Claude Fable 5 and GPT-5.6 Sol.

Kimi with its 1m context loop is great for long document knowledge work: contracts, discovery documents, research literature, financial filings, anything where the 1M token window lets you process an entire corpus in one pass instead of chunking and losing cross references.

Agentic workflows: tool calling, browsing, and multi step reasoning chains where the model plans and executes over long horizons.

K3 scored 91.2 on BrowseComp, a state of the art result for long horizon information seeking.

High volume production inference: because it is sparse MoE with only 16 of 896 experts active per token, the per token cost is far below what the 2.8T parameter count suggests, which makes it economically viable to serve at scale.

So - what does this mean to the buyer?

The customer for rack scale GB300 serving of K3 is not a hobbyist or a small startup (like me). 

It is an organization with three characteristics:

Real production traffic. 

They are already spending heavily on frontier model APIs, or they have an AI product with enough users that token costs are a top line item.

Think coding assistant companies, legal tech platforms, AI search products, and enterprise software vendors embedding agents into their products.

A need for customization and self training.

Because K3 is open weights, they can fine tune it on proprietary data, distill it, or modify it, none of which is possible with a closed API model like the OpenAI or Claudes 

This is important to companies whose differentiation lives in their domain data and not in the training data that was fed to the model.

Companies who have an aversion to lock in. Companies who want the option to move between providers or bring the model in house later. 

Open weights plus a provider like Together AI means the model is portable even if the infrastructure relationship changes.

At the smaller end - if I ever get ther, the same customer profile starts on Together AI's serverless endpoints or an 8 GPU dedicated node, then graduates to rack scale clusters when traffic justifies it.

BUT, and maybe I save the most important thing to last:

I use Kimi through Moonshot's own hosted app, and it is excellent. 

Moonshot is a Beijing based company, and when you send a prompt to the Kimi app or the Kimi API, that data is processed on infrastructure under Chinese jurisdiction. 

For personal use and experimentation, that is a perfectly reasonable tradeoff.  I am personally cool with it

For a business in countries like the US, it often is not.

Running K3 through a US provider like Together AI changes the jurisdiction of the data without changing the model

The practical consequence: a US hospital system, bank, law firm, or defense contractor generally cannot route customer or patient data through a Chinese hosted API, full stop.
 
It does not matter how good the model is. 

But because K3 is open weights, they do not have to choose between the model and the jurisdiction. 

They get the same frontier class model, served onshore, on US soil, under US data protection frameworks, with enterprise contracts and audit trails that their compliance teams can actually sign off on.

That is the REAL significance of the open weights release. 

Moonshot did the R&D, published the weights, and in doing so made it possible for any US provider to offer K3 as a fully domestic product. 

Together AI's rack scale clusters are the hardware story, but the onshore data story is what turns K3 from an impressive demo into something a regulated US enterprise can actually deploy and use cheaper to challenge whatever token burn projects they want to run with OpenAI or Anthropic.

That is the game changer here.

Trapped inside the locked-down Chinese city of Wuhan were 33 Sri Lankan students and their family members, young men and women who had traveled to China to study, now stranded at the epicenter of what the World Health Organization had not yet declared a pandemic. Cut off from their families and unable to leave, they watched the virus close in around them. Back in Sri Lanka, their parents were frantic. The students were terrified. Chinese authorities had sealed the city, commercial flights had stopped, and the airport was closed to normal traffic. Getting into Wuhan was nearly impossible; getting out was supposed to be completely impossible.

President Gotabaya Rajapaksa made the decision to bring them home.

This was neither an obvious nor an easy decision. In late January 2020, very little was known about the virus that would later be named SARS-CoV-2. Its transmission routes were not fully understood, and its fatality rate appeared alarmingly high. There was no vaccine, no standard treatment, and no established protocol for evacuating citizens from a city in the grip of an unknown pathogen. The risk was not theoretical: sending a plane into Wuhan meant sending a flight crew into the epicenter of an outbreak that was killing people daily, with no guarantee that the crew would not contract the virus, no certainty that the evacuees were uninfected, and no guarantee that bringing them home would not introduce the pathogen to Sri Lanka.

Many countries with far greater resources, larger air forces, and more sophisticated public health infrastructure were hesitating, debating, forming committees, and conducting risk assessments while their citizens remained trapped.

Gotabaya did not hesitate. He instructed the Sri Lanka Embassy in Beijing to submit an application to Chinese authorities for permission to land a SriLankan Airlines aircraft at Wuhan Tianhe International Airport, a facility that was, for all practical purposes, closed to the world. The Chinese government, which was granting landing permission to only a handful of nations, expedited Sri Lanka's request, and the flight was approved.

SriLankan Airlines was asked to execute the mission. What happened next is one of the most quietly heroic episodes in the airline's history, though it has been almost entirely forgotten. The airline called for volunteer crew members rather than ordering anyone to fly to Wuhan. Sixteen crew members, including pilots, co-pilots, cabin crew, and engineers, stepped forward and agreed to go.

The Sri Lanka Air Force equipped the crew with Ebola-grade protective gear, including full-body hazmat suits, N95 respirators, eye protection, gloves, and boot covers, and trained them on safe wearing and removal procedures. The photographs from the mission are extraordinary: pilots in full hazmat gear sitting in the cockpit, cabin crew dressed head-to-toe in protective suits greeting terrified students at the gate, and an aircraft cabin configured specifically for a medical evacuation where every surface was sanitized and every protocol was designed to prevent viral transmission.

Flight UL1423 departed for Wuhan, flying toward a city from which the rest of the world was fleeing. It landed at an airport that was essentially a ghost facility, with no commercial flights, no passengers, and no normal operations, just the eerie silence of a locked-down metropolis punctuated by occasional military or charter aircraft conducting evacuations for the few governments that had mustered the courage to send planes.

The 33 Sri Lankan students and their family members boarded the aircraft. They had waited for days, uncertain whether anyone would come, watching as some countries evacuated their citizens while others debated and delayed. Sri Lanka came. A small island nation in the Indian Ocean, with a national airline perpetually in financial difficulty and a defense budget that was a rounding error compared to major powers, sent a plane into the most dangerous city on Earth and brought its people home.

The flight did not return to Bandaranaike International Airport in Colombo. Instead, it landed at Mattala Rajapaksa International Airport, the much-maligned facility in Hambantota that critics had labeled a white elephant, a monument to political vanity, and an empty airport in the middle of nowhere. On February 1st, 2020, that airport served its vital purpose. It was selected precisely because it was remote and far from population centers; its isolation made it the ideal facility for receiving an aircraft from a pandemic epicenter without risking exposure to the general population. The airport that critics had ridiculed turned out to be exactly what the country needed at that moment.

The students were received at Mattala by health authorities and military personnel, transferred to a quarantine facility at the Diyatalawa Army Camp in the central highlands, and monitored for fourteen days under strict medical supervision. Every protocol was followed, every precaution was taken, and not a single student transmitted the virus to the general population. The quarantine was completed successfully, and on February 14th, 2020, which was Valentine's Day, the students were released and reunited with their families.

The crew of Flight UL1423 were hailed as heroes. SriLankan Airlines publicly expressed gratitude to its courageous team, and the nation briefly celebrated their bravery. Then, in a detail that reveals more about the character of these sixteen people than any medal could, the crew declined to accept the special financial bonuses offered by the airline for undertaking the mission. Instead, they asked the airline to use those funds to purchase face masks, gloves, and sanitization equipment for ground staff, including the baggage handlers, cleaners, and check-in agents who worked at the airport daily without protective gear or recognition. The crew who flew into the epicenter asked that the reward for their courage be redirected to those who would never make headlines.

Sri Lanka was among the first countries in the world to successfully evacuate its citizens from Wuhan. Only a handful of nations, including the United States, Japan, South Korea, France, and India, managed to conduct evacuations during that narrow window in late January and early February 2020 before conditions deteriorated further. Most were major powers with vast diplomatic, military, and logistical resources. Sri Lanka was not a major power. It was a small island nation recovering from a devastating Easter Sunday bombing attack less than a year prior, navigating a fragile economy, and led by a newly elected president who had been in office for barely two months. Yet Sri Lanka's plane was among the first to land in Wuhan, among the first to bring its citizens home, and among the first to execute a flawless quarantine protocol that prevented secondary transmission.

This occurred because one leader made a decision without waiting for committees, consultations, risk assessments, or international coordination. Gotabaya Rajapaksa made the right call in this instance. He decided that 33 Sri Lankan students trapped in an outbreak zone were worth the risk, that Sri Lanka would not wait for larger nations to act first, and that bringing citizens home from danger was neither optional nor subject to bureaucratic delay. He issued the order, and a plane flew to Wuhan.

In July 2022, the so-called Aragalaya sent Gotabaya home, calling him "Gota Pissek."

When Pyrrhus crossed into Italy expecting to crush an obscure people beyond the Greek world, he looked across the River Siris and saw, for the first time, the disciplined ranks of the power that would soon master the Mediterranean: 

“The discipline of these ‘barbarians’ is not barbarian at all. We shall see what they can do.”

Decades later, in a war with the Mediterranean power of Carthage, at Cannae, Hannibal annihilated the greatest army these people had ever put to field. Sending emissaries to offer peace, and expecting the defeated Republic to submit as any other power would. 

These Rōmānī refused even to admit them. Their Senate would not permit surrender to be proposed, going as far to ban the word surrender from ever being spoken in the Senate again. 

These Romans began arming boys and slaves to raise new legions from the ruins of the old. For fourteen more years these people from Rome pursued the war, carried it into Africa, crushed the Carthaginian general Hannibal at Zama, stripped Carthage of its empire and, when the final hour came, razed their capitol city itself to the ground.

What these obscure Romans did was conquer all of Italy, crushed the might of Carthage, crossed into Greece, shattered the invincible Macedonian phalanx, quelled the kingdoms of Alexander’s successors, and brought the entire Mediterranean world beneath the authority of the Roman Eagle. A people Greeks had hardly noticed rising. 

With the Greek world broken and Rome standing master over nearly all Greece had once regarded as civilization, Polybius looked upon the astonishing rise of these once-dismissed barbarians and could only marvel: 

“For who is so worthless or indolent as not to wish to know by what means and under what system of polity the Romans in less than fifty-three years have succeeded in subjecting nearly the whole inhabited world to their sole government—a thing unique in history?”

text:
On this day in 1777, the Continental Congress did something that sounds completely insane on paper. They commissioned a nineteen-year-old French aristocrat with zero combat experience as a major general in the American army. His name was the Marquis de Lafayette, and betting on him turned out to be one of the best decisions they ever made.

Understand how unlikely this was. Lafayette was a teenager, rich, titled, and green as grass, who had defied his own king and slipped out of France against orders to come fight for a revolution that was losing. Congress was drowning in foreign officers demanding rank and money, and they were sick of it. What set Lafayette apart was a single line in his offer: he would serve at his own expense and take no pay. He did not want money. He wanted the cause. That, plus a letter backed by Benjamin Franklin, flipped Congress from annoyed to charmed.

The gamble paid off almost immediately. Just weeks later at the Battle of Brandywine, this untested kid general was shot through the leg, and instead of going down he stayed up rallying retreating troops, helping turn a rout into an orderly withdrawal before he would let anyone treat the wound. Washington, who had lost his own son years earlier, more or less adopted him. The feeling was mutual.

And here is why July 31 matters. That teenager grew into one of the most important men of the entire Revolution. Four years later it was Lafayette, maneuvering across Virginia, who helped pin Cornwallis at Yorktown and set up the victory that won the war. The old commanders trusted a nineteen-year-old volunteer with a general's stars, and he spent the rest of the war proving they were right.

Surveillance video later released by police shows the group approaching the location. Some reports noted the use of handguns and rifles.

Surbezz Clark, 53, of Chicago, and Carlos A. Jones, 46, of Chicago, were pronounced dead at the University of Chicago Medical Center. The Cook County medical examiner’s office confirmed the deaths. The Chicago Police Department’s Area Two detectives are investigating under case number JK316902. No arrests have been made.
